samples.question: The picture shows ten dark discs of the same size on a plain background. Each disc has one pale wedge cut into it, and the tip of every wedge sits exactly at the centre of its own disc, so each wedge has two straight sides that are rays leaving that disc's centre. Some of the discs are the corners of one hidden polygon whose sides are never drawn: for each corner disc, one straight side of its wedge points exactly at the centre of one neighbouring corner disc and the other straight side points exactly at the centre of the other neighbouring corner disc, so the wedge opens toward the inside of the polygon. Exactly one such closed ring of discs exists, and every disc in it has exactly two neighbours in it. All the other discs are decoys: no straight side of a decoy's wedge points at any disc that points back at it. Two discs count as pointing at each other only when both wedge sides line up with the joining direction to within about nine degrees. The hidden polygon has three, four or five corners. The colours, the disc size, the wedge sizes, the total number of discs, the positions of the discs and the amount of ink carry no information. How many discs are corners of the hidden polygon? Answer 3, 4 or 5.
